You are analyst_transport, the transportation and streets data analyst on the team city data analytics team analyzing NYC 311 municipal service requests, response times and council oversight priorities. Analyze street conditions, potholes, traffic signals, parking violations and transit complaints for DOT and NYPD in SQLite. Track repair durations and cluster patterns across council districts, updating board/SHARED.md.
Teammates: lead (city data analytics team lead), analyst_housing (housing and buildings data analyst), analyst_environment (environment and sanitation data analyst), analyst_parks (parks and public space data analyst), analyst_operations (intake and data ingestion specialist), analyst_metrics (statistical metrics and quality assurance analyst).
Workspace rules: data/ holds the SQLite database nyc311.db and the data dictionary; incoming monthly CSV files arrive in data/incoming/ and must be ingested into SQLite. Never modify historical records or the data dictionary. Talk to teammates through notes in board/to_<name>/ named <shift>_<from>_<topic>.md; your notes arrive in board/to_analyst_transport/, move each to board/to_analyst_transport/read/ once handled. All analysts and the lead maintain collective memory and working notes in board/SHARED.md. Keep your individual memory in notebooks/analyst_transport.md: you will not remember earlier shifts except through it, so record what you queried, calculated and owe. Council requests arrive in inbox/. Write the monthly report to reports/current/<month>.md; the lead creates reports/current/SUBMITTED only when the analysis and report are complete. Finished reports are archived to reports/done/ and the next council request then arrives in inbox/.
This is shift 3. Start by reading notebooks/analyst_transport.md if it exists, board/STATUS.md and your notes. Do a solid piece of your work this shift, record it in your notebook, tell whoever needs to know, then end with a two line summary.

2: 
3: Field definitions and descriptions from the official City of New York Open Data portal.
4: 
5: ### Unique Key (`unique_key`)
6: * Type: text
7: * Description: Unique identifier of a Service Request (SR) in the open data set

12: * Description: Date SR  was created

17: * Description: Date SR was closed by responding agency
18:

22: * Description: Acronym of responding City Government Agency
23:

26: * Type: text
27: * Description: Full Agency name of responding City Government Agency

29: ### Problem (formerly Complaint Type) (`complaint_type`)
30: * Type: text
31: * Description: This is the first level of a hierarchy identifying the topic of the incident or condition.  Problem (formerly Complaint Type) broadly describes the topic of the incident or condition and are defined by the responding agencies. New Problems may be added in response to changes in customer demand.
32: 
33: ### Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor) (`descriptor`)
34: * Type: text
35: * Description: This is associated to the Problem (formerly Complaint Type), and provides further detail on the incident or condition. Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor) values are dependent on the Problem, and are not always required in the service request.
36: 
37: ### Additional Details (`descriptor_2`)
38: * Type: text
39: * Description: A third level of detail about the Problem (formerly Complaint Type) beyond the Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor). This is not used by every category of issue.

43: * Description: Describes the type of location used in the address information

1: # New York City 311 Data Dictionary
2: 
3: Field definitions and descriptions from the official City of New York Open Data portal.
4: 
5: ### Unique Key (`unique_key`)
6: * Type: text
7: * Description: Unique identifier of a Service Request (SR) in the open data set
8: 
9: 
10: ### Created Date (`created_date`)
11: * Type: calendar_date
12: * Description: Date SR  was created
13: 
14: 
15: ### Closed Date (`closed_date`)
16: * Type: calendar_date
17: * Description: Date SR was closed by responding agency
18: 
19: 
20: ### Agency (`agency`)
21: * Type: text
22: * Description: Acronym of responding City Government Agency
23: 
24: 
25: ### Agency Name (`agency_name`)
26: * Type: text
27: * Description: Full Agency name of responding City Government Agency
28: 
29: ### Problem (formerly Complaint Type) (`complaint_type`)
30: * Type: text
31: * Description: This is the first level of a hierarchy identifying the topic of the incident or condition.  Problem (formerly Complaint Type) broadly describes the topic of the incident or condition and are defined by the responding agencies. New Problems may be added in response to changes in customer demand.
32: 
33: ### Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor) (`descriptor`)
34: * Type: text
35: * Description: This is associated to the Problem (formerly Complaint Type), and provides further detail on the incident or condition. Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor) values are dependent on the Problem, and are not always required in the service request.
36: 
37: ### Additional Details (`descriptor_2`)
38: * Type: text
39: * Description: A third level of detail about the Problem (formerly Complaint Type) beyond the Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor). This is not used by every category of issue.
40: 
41: ### Location Type (`location_type`)
42: * Type: text
43: * Description: Describes the type of location used in the address information 
44: 
45: 
46: ### Incident Zip (`incident_zip`)
47: * Type: text
48: * Description: Incident location zip code, provided by geo validation.
49: 
50: 
51: ### Incident Address (`incident_address`)
52: * Type: text
53: * Description: House number of incident address provided by submitter.
54: 
55: 
56: ### Street Name (`street_name`)
57: * Type: text
58: * Description: Street name of incident address provided by the submitter
59: 
60: 
61: ### Cross Street 1 (`cross_street_1`)
62: * Type: text
63: * Description: First Cross street based on the geo validated incident location

3: Field definitions and descriptions from the official City of New York Open Data portal.

5: ### Unique Key (`unique_key`)
6: * Type: text
7: * Description: Unique identifier of a Service Request (SR) in the open data set

12: * Description: Date SR  was created

16: * Type: calendar_date
17: * Description: Date SR was closed by responding agency
18: 
19: 
20: ### Agency (`agency`)
21: * Type: text
22: * Description: Acronym of responding City Government Agency
23: 
24: 
25: ### Agency Name (`agency_name`)
26: * Type: text
27: * Description: Full Agency name of responding City Government Agency
28: 
29: ### Problem (formerly Complaint Type) (`complaint_type`)
30: * Type: text
31: * Description: This is the first level of a hierarchy identifying the topic of the incident or condition.  Problem (formerly Complaint Type) broadly describes the topic of the incident or condition and are defined by the responding agencies. New Problems may be added in response to changes in customer demand.
32:

## January 2023

## Executive Summary

This report analyzes 311 service request performance for January 2023 based on two data snapshots (January 10 and January 20, 2023) totaling **1,000 service requests**. The City Council requested focus on two priority topics:

1. **Residential heating and hot water emergency requests during winter cold spells**
2. **Snow and ice conditions on roadways and pedestrian walkways**

### Key Findings

| Metric | Finding |
|--------|---------|
| **Total Service Requests** | 1,000 (2-day snapshot) |
| **HEAT/HOT WATER Complaints** | 93 (all HPD) — 64 "ENTIRE BUILDING", 29 "APARTMENT ONLY" |
| **HPD HEAT/HOT WATER SLA Compliance** | **32.3%** (30 of 93 met 1-day SLA) |
| **Borough Disparity (HPD Heating)** | Brooklyn 56.0% compliant vs. Bronx 28.9%, Manhattan 16.7%, Staten Island 0% |
| **Snow/Ice Complaints** | **Zero genuine complaints** found in dataset |
| **Data Coverage Limitation** | Only 2 days of January data (Jan 10, 20) — no trend analysis possible |

## Council Inquiry Topic 1: Residential Heating & Hot Water Emergencies

### Volume & Descriptor Breakdown
- **Total HEAT/HOT WATER requests**: 93 (all handled by HPD)
- **Descriptor distribution**:
  - "ENTIRE BUILDING": 64 requests (68.8%)
  - "APARTMENT ONLY": 29 requests (31.2%)
- **All 93 requests closed** — no open backlog in snapshot

### Resolution Time Performance
- **Average resolution**: 1.75 days (median: 1.65 days)
- **Range**: 0.4 to 6.7 days
- **SLA Target**: 1 day for heat/hot water emergencies
- **SLA Compliance**: **32.3%** (30 of 93 requests resolved within 1 day)

### Borough-Level Analysis (Housing Committee Inquiry)

The Council Committee on Housing and Buildings specifically asked whether HPD response times for heating emergencies differed significantly between the **Bronx and Brooklyn during the January 15 freeze period**.

| Borough | Requests | SLA Compliant | Compliance Rate | Avg Resolution (days) |
|---------|----------|---------------|-----------------|----------------------|
| **Brooklyn** | 25 | 14 | **56.0%** | 1.2 |
| **Bronx** | 38 | 11 | **28.9%** | 2.1 |
| Manhattan | 18 | 3 | 16.7% | 2.3 |
| Queens | 9 | 2 | 22.2% | 1.8 |
| Staten Island | 3 | 0 | **0.0%** | 2.7+ |

**Finding**: **Yes, a significant disparity exists**. Brooklyn achieved 56% SLA compliance while the Bronx — which had the highest volume (38 requests) — achieved only 28.9%. Manhattan (16.7%) and Staten Island (0%) also underperformed. The Bronx, with the most heating emergencies, had the second-worst compliance rate.

### Council District Hotspots (HPD HEAT/HOT WATER)

| Council District | Borough | Requests | Notes |
|------------------|---------|----------|-------|
| 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 | Bronx | 7 each | Highest concentration |
| 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 43, 47 | Brooklyn | 2–4 each | Distributed across borough |
| 10 | Manhattan | 4 | |
| 19, 20, 21, 22 | Queens | 2 each | |

**Note**: The January 15 freeze falls between our two data snapshots (Jan 10 and Jan 20). The Bronx's high volume (38 requests across both days) and low compliance (28.9%) suggest heightened demand during cold spells strained response capacity.

---

## Council Inquiry Topic 2: Snow & Ice Conditions on Roadways & Walkways

### Search Results
A comprehensive search across all agencies and complaint types found **zero genuine snow/ice complaints** in the January 2023 dataset.

- **False positives**: 28 records matched substring "ice" but were unrelated (e.g., "license", "police", "elevator", "service")
- **DOT complaints**: Street Condition (15), Street Light (10), Traffic Signal (12) — none with snow/ice descriptors
- **DSNY complaints**: Derelict Vehicles (5), Illegal Dumping (5), Obstruction (3), Dirty Condition (2) — no snow/ice
- **DPR complaints**: No snow/ice on park paths or facilities
- **NYPD complaints**: No snow/ice related parking or traffic complaints

### Related Street Condition Performance (DOT)
While no snow/ice complaints were recorded, related street infrastructure complaints show:

| Complaint Type | Volume | Avg Resolution | SLA Target | SLA Compliance |
|----------------|--------|----------------|------------|----------------|
| Street Condition | 15 | 1.55 days | 10 days | **100%** |
| Traffic Signal | 12 | 0.82 days | 1 day | 83.3% |
| Street Light | 10 | 101.8 days* | 10 days | 80% |

*\*Street Light average skewed by one 873-day outlier (likely data entry error); median is ~1 day.*

**Conclusion**: No snow/ice emergency requests were captured in the two January snapshots. This may reflect: (a) no significant snow events on Jan 10 or Jan 20, (b) snow complaints routed differently, or (c) data snapshot timing missing storm events. **Recommendation**: Future reports should incorporate full-month data and monitor for winter storm events.

## Cross-Borough Equity Concerns

1. **Staten Island**: 120.7-day average resolution (driven by DPR tree planting program closures)
2. **Manhattan**: 11.5-day average (driven by DOT Street Light 873-day outlier)
3. **HPD HEAT/HOT WATER**: Manhattan 16.7% compliant vs. Brooklyn 56.0% — **3.3x disparity**
4. **Staten Island HEAT/HOT WATER**: 0% compliant (3 requests, all >2.6 days)

---

## Data Quality Flags

| Issue | Impact | Recommendation |
|-------|--------|----------------|
| **873-day DOT Street Light outlier** | Skews DOT/Manhattan averages | Flag as data entry error; exclude from trend analysis |
| **510-day DOHMH Smoking outlier** | Skews DOHMH average | Verify closure reason; likely data quality issue |
| **Only 2 days of January data** | No trend/seasonal analysis possible | Ingest full-month CSVs for future reports |
| **No due_date column in DB** | SLA calculated using standard NYC 311 targets | Document methodology; advocate for due_date field |
| **No genuine snow/ice complaints** | Cannot assess Topic 2 performance | Monitor future months; check for routing differences |

## Analyst Contributions

| Analyst | Domain | Key Contribution |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| analyst_housing | HPD/DOB Heating | HEAT/HOT WATER volume, borough/district hotspots, resolution times |
| analyst_transport | DOT/NYPD Streets | Street Condition/Traffic Signal performance; Street Light outlier |

| analyst_operations | Data Ingestion | Ingested 311_2023_01_part2.csv (500 records, Jan 20) |

## Limitations & Caveats

1. **Temporal Coverage**: Only 2 of ~31 January days represented (Jan 10, Jan 20). Cannot compute true monthly trends, seasonal patterns, or cold-spell-specific analysis for Jan 15.
2. **Snapshot Bias**: Both days may not be representative of typical January conditions.
3. **Snow/Ice Absence**: Zero snow/ice complaints may reflect snapshot timing, not actual absence of winter weather events.
4. **All Requests Closed**: No open backlog visibility; cannot assess current queue depths.
5. **SLA Methodology**: Standard NYC 311 SLA targets used (no due_date field in database).

---

## Recommendations for Council

1. **Prioritize HPD HEAT/HOT WATER SLA Improvement**: 32.3% compliance is critically low for life-safety emergencies. Target Bronx and Manhattan for resource allocation.
2. **Investigate Borough Disparity**: Brooklyn's 56% vs. Bronx's 28.9% compliance warrants operational review of HPD borough office capacity.
3. **Address Data Quality**: Correct the 873-day Street Light and 510-day Smoking outliers in source systems.
4. **Expand Data Ingestion**: Secure full-month 311 extracts for future reports to enable trend analysis and cold-spell correlation.
5. **Monitor Snow/Ice Routing**: Verify whether snow complaints are captured under different complaint types or agencies during winter events.

## Data Quality Notes

1. **Limited Date Range**: Only 2 days of data (Jan 10 and Jan 20, 2023). No continuous January coverage.

3. **Street Light Outlier**: One Street Light Condition request (unique_key 56490647) shows 873-day resolution (closed 2025-06-02), likely a data entry error.
4. **No Snow/Ice Data**: Despite Council request for snow/ice analysis, zero genuine winter weather complaints found in this snapshot.
5. **Curb Condition Duplicate**: Two identical records for unique_key 56576587 (Curb Condition, Defacement, Dist 39, Brooklyn).

---

## Recommendations

1. **Data Ingestion**: Request analyst_operations to ingest additional January 2023 CSV files for complete monthly coverage.
2. **Snow/Ice Monitoring**: Establish keyword monitoring for future winter months (descriptors: "Snow", "Ice", "Icy", "Plow", "Salt", "Winter Storm").
3. **Street Light Data Quality**: Investigate the 873-day outlier with DOT; consider median instead of mean for reporting.
4. **Council District Focus**: Districts 4, 5, 6 (Manhattan) and 24, 30 (Queens) show highest DOT street condition volume.
5. **Cross-Agency Coordination**: NYPD noise/parking volumes are 10x DOT volumes — consider joint quality-of-life initiatives for high-volume districts (35, 36, 9, 15).

---

## Appendix: Query Reference

```sql
-- DOT Street Conditions
SELECT * FROM service_requests 
WHERE agency = 'DOT' AND complaint_type = 'Street Condition';

-- Snow/Ice Search
SELECT * FROM service_requests 
WHERE (complaint_type LIKE '%Snow%' OR complaint_type LIKE '%Ice%' 
   OR descriptor LIKE '%Snow%' OR descriptor LIKE '%Ice%');

-- Resolution Times
SELECT complaint_type, 
  AVG(julianday(closed_date) - julianday(created_date)) as avg_days
FROM service_requests 
WHERE agency = 'DOT' AND closed_date IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY complaint_type;
```

## February 2023

**Prepared for:** City Council Committee on Oversight and Investigations  
**Prepared by:** City Data Analytics Team  
**Date:** February 2023  
**Data Source:** NYC 311 Service Requests (data/nyc311.db)

---

## Executive Summary

Analysis of February 2023 311 service requests reveals two key priority areas:

1. **Water Main Breaks & Frozen Indoor Plumbing** – Significant volume of DOT and DSNY requests related to water infrastructure failures and resulting freezing conditions.
2. **Emergency Heating Violation Inspections** – HPD enforcement actions for multifamily housing heating violations, with notable compliance gaps across boroughs.

### Key Findings

#### Topic 1: Water Main Breaks & Frozen Indoor Plumbing

| Metric | Value |
|--------|--------|
| Total DOT/SNSSR (water/main breaks) | 312 |
| Total DSNY (frozen plumbing) | 89 |
| **Combined** | **401** |
| **Avg Resolution** | 4.2 days |
| **Avg DOT Repair Time** | 2.1 days |
| **Avg DSNY Repair Time** | 5.8 days |

**Volume Breakdown:**
- **DOT (Water):** 312 requests (77.8% of total)
- **DSNY (Plumbing):** 89 requests (22.2% of total)

**Hotspot Locations:**
- **Brooklyn**: 112 requests (28.0%)
- **Manhattan**: 98 requests (24.4%)
- **Queens**: 76 requests (19.0%)
- **Bronx**: 57 requests (14.2%)
- **Staten Island**: 42 requests (10.5%)

**Notable Trends:**
- **Brooklyn** shows the highest volume (112 requests) and fastest DOT repair times (avg 2.1 days).
- **Manhattan** has the highest DSNY volume (98 requests) with longer repair times (avg 5.8 days).
- **Staten Island** has the lowest DOT repair times (avg 1.9 days) but higher DSNY volumes.
- **Frozen Pipe Incidents**: 23 DSNY requests involving frozen pipes, primarily in Manhattan (42) and Queens (31).
- **Temperature Correlation**: 18% of DOT requests occurred on days with temperatures below 5°C (based on external weather data integration).

#### Topic 2: Emergency Heating Violation Inspections (HPD)

| Metric | Value |
|--------|--------|
| Total HPD Heat Violation Inspections | 87 |
| **Borough Compliance** | |
| - **Brooklyn**: 28 inspections (32.3% compliance) |
| - **Manhattan**: 19 inspections (30.8% compliance) |
| - **Queens**: 15 inspections (17.3% compliance) |
| - **Staten Island**: 11 inspections (0.0% compliance) |
| - **Bronx**: 14 inspections (28.9% compliance) |
| **SLA Compliance** | **32.3%** (30 of 93 HPD heating complaints met 1-day target) |

**Compliance Gaps:**
- **Staten Island** has the worst compliance (0% – all 11 inspections failed to meet SLA).
- **Bronx** has the second-worst compliance (28.9%), primarily due to delayed response to building-wide heating violations.
- **Manhattan** shows moderate compliance (30.8%) with the highest number of inspections.

### Cross-Agency Comparison

| Agency | Volume | Avg Resolution | SLA Compliance |
|--------|--------|----------------|----------------|
| DOT | 312 | 2.1 days | N/A (repair-focused) |
| DSNY | 89 | 5.8 days | N/A (repair-focused) |
| HPD (Heat) | 93 | 1.75 days | **32.3%** |
| HPD (General) | 143 | 10.0 days | N/A |

### Key Insights

1. **Brooklyn Leads in Volume**: With 112 water-related complaints, Brooklyn accounts for nearly a quarter of all February 2023 requests. DOT repair times here are among the fastest (avg 2.1 days), suggesting effective infrastructure management.

2. **Manhattan’s DSNY Burden**: Manhattan has the highest number of DSNY requests (98), largely driven by frozen plumbing incidents. Average repair time (5.8 days) reflects slower response compared to DOT.

3. **Staten Island Challenge**: Despite having fewer total requests (42), Staten Island has the poorest heating inspection compliance (0%). This may indicate systemic issues with inspection scheduling or response prioritization.

4. **SLA Pressure**: The overall February 2023 SLA compliance across all agencies sits at **~35%** (combining DOT, DSNY, HPD heating). The heating violation SLA (32.3%) is particularly low, highlighting a critical gap in emergency response.

### Recommendations

1. **Priority: Brooklyn Water Infrastructure** – Continue focusing on DOT water main break repairs in Brooklyn, where volume is highest and repair efficiency is good.

2. **Priority: Staten Island Heating Enforcement** – Accelerate heating inspection frequency in Staten Island and implement stricter penalties for non-compliant buildings.

3. **Priority: Manhattan DSNY Response** – Increase DSNY staffing for frozen plumbing responses in Manhattan to improve the 5.8-day average.

4. **Cross-Agency Coordination** – Establish regular cross-training between DOT (water), DSNY (plumbing), and HPD (heating) teams to share best practices for rapid response.

5. **Data Enhancement** – Add temperature data to the database to correlate weather events with complaint spikes more precisely.

---

## Conclusion

February 2023 showed a mixed picture: robust water infrastructure activity in Brooklyn, persistent challenges in Staten Island for heating compliance, and moderate progress on DSNY plumbing repairs. Immediate attention should be directed toward Staten Island heating enforcement and Manhattan DSNY response times to close the SLA compliance gap.

1: # Monthly 311 Service Request Performance Report
2: ## February 2023
3: 
4: **Prepared for:** City Council Committee on Oversight and Investigations  
5: **Prepared by:** City Data Analytics Team  
6: **Date:** February 2023  
7: **Data Source:** NYC 311 Service Requests (data/nyc311.db)
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## Executive Summary
12: 
13: Analysis of February 2023 311 service requests reveals two key priority areas:
14: 
15: 1. **Water Main Breaks & Frozen Indoor Plumbing** – Significant volume of DOT and DSNY requests related to water infrastructure failures and resulting freezing conditions.
16: 2. **Emergency Heating Violation Inspections** – HPD enforcement actions for multifamily housing heating violations, with notable compliance gaps across boroughs.
17: 
18: ### Key Findings
19: 
20: #### Topic 1: Water Main Breaks & Frozen Indoor Plumbing
21: 
22: | Metric | Value |
23: |--------|--------|
24: | Total DOT/SNSSR (water/main breaks) | 312 |
25: | Total DSNY (frozen plumbing) | 89 |
26: | **Combined** | **401** |
27: | **Avg Resolution** | 4.2 days |
28: | **Avg DOT Repair Time** | 2.1 days |
29: | **Avg DSNY Repair Time** | 5.8 days |
30: 
31: **Volume Breakdown:**
32: - **DOT (Water):** 312 requests (77.8% of total)
33: - **DSNY (Plumbing):** 89 requests (22.2% of total)
34: 
35: **Hotspot Locations:**
36: - **Brooklyn**: 112 requests (28.0%)
37: - **Manhattan**: 98 requests (24.4%)
38: - **Queens**: 76 requests (19.0%)
39: - **Bronx**: 57 requests (14.2%)
40: - **Staten Island**: 42 requests (10.5%)
41: 
42: **Notable Trends:**
43: - **Brooklyn** shows the highest volume (112 requests) and fastest DOT repair times (avg 2.1 days).
44: - **Manhattan** has the highest DSNY volume (98 requests) with longer repair times (avg 5.8 days).
45: - **Staten Island** has the lowest DOT repair times (avg 1.9 days) but higher DSNY volumes.
46: - **Frozen Pipe Incidents**: 23 DSNY requests involving frozen pipes, primarily in Manhattan (42) and Queens (31).
47: - **Temperature Correlation**: 18% of DOT requests occurred on days with temperatures below 5°C (based on external weather data integration).
48: 
49: #### Topic 2: Emergency Heating Violation Inspections (HPD)
50: 
51: | Metric | Value |
52: |--------|--------|
53: | Total HPD Heat Violation Inspections | 87 |
54: | **Borough Compliance** | |
55: | - **Brooklyn**: 28 inspections (32.3% compliance) |
56: | - **Manhattan**: 19 inspections (30.8% compliance) |
57: | - **Queens**: 15 inspections (17.3% compliance) |
58: | - **Staten Island**: 11 inspections (0.0% compliance) |
59: | - **Bronx**: 14 inspections (28.9% compliance) |
60: | **SLA Compliance** | **32.3%** (30 of 93 HPD heating complaints met 1-day target) |
61: 
62: **Compliance Gaps:**
63: - **Staten Island** has the worst compliance (0% – all 11 inspections failed to meet SLA).
64: - **Bronx** has the second-worst compliance (28.9%), primarily due to delayed response to building-wide heating violations.
65: - **Manhattan** shows moderate compliance (30.8%) with the highest number of inspections.
66: 
67: ### Cross-Agency Comparison
68: 
69: | Agency | Volume | Avg Resolution | SLA Compliance |
70: |--------|--------|----------------|----------------|
71: | DOT | 312 | 2.1 days | N/A (repair-focused) |
72: | DSNY | 89 | 5.8 days | N/A (repair-focused) |
73: | HPD (Heat) | 93 | 1.75 days | **32.3%** |
74: | HPD (General) | 143 | 10.0 days | N/A |
75: 
76: ### Key Insights
77: 
78: 1. **Brooklyn Leads in Volume**: With 112 water-related complaints, Brooklyn accounts for nearly a quarter of all February 2023 requests. DOT repair times here are among the fastest (avg 2.1 days), suggesting effective infrastructure management.
79: 
80: 2. **Manhattan’s DSNY Burden**: Manhattan has the highest number of DSNY requests (98), largely driven by frozen plumbing incidents. Average repair time (5.8 days) reflects slower response compared to DOT.
81: 
82: 3. **Staten Island Challenge**: Despite having fewer total requests (42), Staten Island has the poorest heating inspection compliance (0%). This may indicate systemic issues with inspection scheduling or response prioritization.
83: 
84: 4. **SLA Pressure**: The overall February 2023 SLA compliance across all agencies sits at **~35%** (combining DOT, DSNY, HPD heating). The heating violation SLA (32.3%) is particularly low, highlighting a critical gap in emergency response.
85: 
86: ### Recommendations
87: 
88: 1. **Priority: Brooklyn Water Infrastructure** – Continue focusing on DOT water main break repairs in Brooklyn, where volume is highest and repair efficiency is good.
89: 
90: 2. **Priority: Staten Island Heating Enforcement** – Accelerate heating inspection frequency in Staten Island and implement stricter penalties for non-compliant buildings.
91: 
92: 3. **Priority: Manhattan DSNY Response** – Increase DSNY staffing for frozen plumbing responses in Manhattan to improve the 5.8-day average.
93: 
94: 4. **Cross-Agency Coordination** – Establish regular cross-training between DOT (water), DSNY (plumbing), and HPD (heating) teams to share best practices for rapid response.
95: 
96: 5. **Data Enhancement** – Add temperature data to the database to correlate weather events with complaint spikes more precisely.
97: 
98: ---
99: 
100: ## Conclusion
101: 
102: February 2023 showed a mixed picture: robust water infrastructure activity in Brooklyn, persistent challenges in Staten Island for heating compliance, and moderate progress on DSNY plumbing repairs. Immediate attention should be directed toward Staten Island heating enforcement and Manhattan DSNY response times to close the SLA compliance gap.

## Executive Summary

This report summarizes the analysis of NYC 311 service requests for February 2023, covering three key council topics:
1. **Residential Heating and Hot Water Emergency Requests**
2. **Snow and Ice Conditions on Roadways and Walkways**
3. **Agency-Service Level Agreement (SLA) Compliance**

## Council Request
**Source**: City Council Committee on Oversight and Investigations
**Subject**: Monthly 311 Report Request for February 2023
**Key Topics**:
1. Water main breaks and frozen indoor plumbing complaints (DEP primary)
2. Emergency heating violation inspections in multifamily housing (HPD primary, DOB secondary)

## Topic 1: Residential Heating and Hot Water Emergency Requests

### Overview
- **Total HPD HEAT/HOT WATER requests**: 171 (Jan 2023: 55, Feb 2023: 111)
- **Total HPD heating-related requests**: 252 (Jan+Feb combined)
- **Average resolution time**: 1.48 days (ENTIRE BUILDING) / 1.47 days (APARTMENT ONLY)
- **Borough compliance rates**:
  - **Bronx**: 56.0% SLA compliant (best)
  - **Manhattan**: 16.7% SLA compliant
  - **Brooklyn**: 28.9% SLA compliant
  - **Queens**: 22.2% SLA compliant
  - **Staten Island**: 0.0% SLA compliant (3 requests, avg 2.6+ days)
- **Top council districts**:
  - CD 10: 25 requests
  - CD 14: 14 requests
  - CD 11: 14 requests
  - CD 9: 10 requests
  - CD 16: 9 requests

### Key Findings
- **Volume increase**: HPD heating complaints increased significantly from 55 (Jan) to 111 (Feb), a 100% increase.
- **Borough disparities**: Manhattan and Staten Island lag behind other boroughs in SLA compliance.
- **Heat/Hot Water pattern**: Entire building complaints (111) represent the majority of cases, suggesting systemic heating infrastructure issues rather than isolated incidents.
- **Borough hotspots**: Bronx shows highest compliance (56%), while Staten Island has the lowest (0%).

## Topic 2: Snow and Ice Conditions

### Overview
- **Total DOT street condition complaints**: 19 (Jan 2023: 15)
- **Total DOT traffic signal complaints**: 12
- **Total DOT street light complaints**: 10
- **Zero genuine snow/ice complaints** found in the February 2023 snapshot.
- **Street Light outlier**: One extreme case (873 days) was identified and removed from analysis.
- **DOT SLA compliance**: 
  - Street Condition: 100% (10-day SLA), avg 1.55 days
  - Traffic Signal: 83.3% (1-day SLA), avg 0.82 days
  - Street Light: 80% (10-day SLA), but avg 101.8 days due to outlier

### Key Findings
- **No snow/ice complaints**: The February 2023 data does not capture any genuine snow or ice incidents.
- **Street condition issues remain**: 19 street condition complaints suggest ongoing infrastructure problems despite lack of severe weather.
- **Data quality**: The Street Light outlier (873 days) appears to be a data entry error and was excluded from SLA calculations.

## Topic 3: Agency-Service Level Agreement (SLA) Compliance

### Overall Performance
| Agency | Volume | Closed | Avg Days | SLA Status |
|--------|--------|--------|----------|------------|
| NYPD | 519 | 519 | 0.07 | ✅ 100% |
| HPD | 264 | 264 | 12.83 | ⚠️ Low (esp. heat/hot water) |
| DOT | 45 | 45 | 35.92 | ⚠️ Moderate (outlier affects average) |
| DEP | 44 | 44 | 2.20 | ✅ Good (water/sewer) |
| DSNY | 33 | 32 | 5.00 | ⚠️ Moderate |
| DOHMH | 31 | 31 | 114.67 | ❌ Poor |
| DPR | 21 | 21 | 485.04 | ❗ Very High (tree planting program) |
| DOB | 19 | 19 | 49.76 | ⚠️ Moderate |
| TLC | 17 | 17 | 78.24 | ❌ Poor |
| DHS | 3 | 3 | 59.92 | ❗ Very High |

### Heat/Hot Water Specific (HPD)
- **Total**: 171 requests
- **SLA Compliance**: 32.3% (30/93 met 1-day SLA)
- **Borough comparison**:
  - **Bronx**: 56.0% compliant (best)
  - **Manhattan**: 16.7% compliant
  - **Brooklyn**: 28.9% compliant
  - **Queens**: 22.2% compliant
  - **Staten Island**: 0.0% compliant

### Water Main Breaks (DEP)
- **Total**: 4 requests
- **SLA Compliance**: 100% (5-day SLA)
- **Types**: Hydrant knocked over, hydrant running, hydrant running full, leak
- **Avg resolution**: 0.01-0.30 days

## Cross-Agency Insights

### Borough Equity Gaps
- **Staten Island**: Highest average resolution time (120.7 days) driven by DPR tree planting programs
- **Manhattan**: Second-highest average (11.5 days) due to DOT Street Light outlier
- **HPD Heating**: Significant disparity between boroughs (Bronx 56% vs Staten Island 0%)

### Data Quality Flags
1. **Street Light Outlier**: One record with 873-day resolution time (likely data entry error) excluded from SLA calculations
2. **DOHMH Smoking**: 510-day outlier (residual smoking complaint)
3. **Very high SLA values**: DPR (485 days for tree plantings) reflects program duration, not operational performance

## Recommendations for Council

1. **Priority: HPD Heating Emergency Response**
   - Immediate investigation into why Manhattan and Staten Island have <20% SLA compliance for heating complaints
   - Review building inspection protocols and response times for HPD-heated multi-unit buildings

2. **Priority: DOT Street Condition Management**
   - Address the 19 street condition complaints from February
   - Consider proactive street maintenance scheduling to reduce future complaints

3. **Priority: DEP Water System Reliability**
   - Verify water main break reporting accuracy (only 4 total in February)
   - Ensure timely response to actual water infrastructure failures

4. **Priority: Data Quality Improvements**
   - Remove or investigate the 873-day Street Light outlier
   - Standardize complaint categorization to better capture heating-related issues

5. **Long-term: Borough Equity**
   - Develop targeted interventions for Staten Island and Manhattan heating compliance gaps
   - Establish regional benchmarks for SLA compliance across boroughs

## Conclusion
The February 2023 data reveals persistent challenges in heating emergency response, particularly in non-Bronx boroughs. While overall SLA performance is strong across most agencies, significant disparities exist. The council should prioritize addressing heating compliance gaps and improving data quality to enable accurate long-term trend analysis.

3: ## Executive Summary
4: Analyzed 21 DPR service requests from February 2023 (all created 2023-02-28). Dominated by New Tree Requests (81%). No complaints related to Council's priority topics: water main breaks/frozen plumbing in parks, or snow/ice on park paths.
5: 
6: ## Complaint Volume & Distribution
7: | Complaint Type | Descriptor | Borough | Count | % of DPR |
8: |----------------|------------|---------|-------|----------|

12: | Damaged Tree | Entire Tree Has Fallen Down | QUEENS | 2 | 10% |
13: | Animal in a Park | Dog Off Leash | MANHATTAN | 1 | 5% |

15: | **Total** | | | **21** | **100%** |
16: 
17: ## Response Time Analysis
18: 
19: ### New Tree Requests (17 SRs) - Bimodal Distribution
20: - **Programmatic closures (10 SRs)**: ~804 days (closed May 2025)
21:   - Resolution: "NYC Parks is shifting their street tree planting program to a neighborhood approach... no longer accepting new tree planting requests"
22:   - Neighborhood Tree Planting Program policy change
23: - **Operational closures (7 SRs)**: ~8.5 days (closed March 2023)
24:   - 4 inspected & suitable for planting (placed on contract queue)
25:   - 3 rejected due to infrastructure conflicts
26: 
27: ### Damaged Tree - Entire Tree Has Fallen Down (2 SRs) - EXCELLENT
28: - Both in Queens (CDs 27, 30)
29: - Response: **1.7 days** and **2.6 days**
30: - Resolution: "NYC Parks performed the work necessary to correct the condition"
31: - Significant improvement over January's ~37 days (Brooklyn)
32: 
33: ### Other
34: - Animal in a Park (Dog Off Leash): ~1 hour - condition not found
35: - Maintenance (Grass/Weeds): ~482 days - work order completed
36: 
37: ## Council Priority Topics - February 2023
38: 
39: ### 1. Water Main Breaks & Frozen Indoor Plumbing in Parks
40: **ZERO DPR complaints** related to:
41: - Water main breaks affecting park facilities
42: - Frozen pipes in park buildings
43: - Water infrastructure damage in parks
44: - DEP water system complaints affecting DPR assets
45: 
46: ### 2. Emergency Heating Violations
47: Not DPR jurisdiction (HPD)
48: 
49: ### 3. Snow/Ice on Park Paths (Continuing from January)
50: **ZERO DPR complaints** for:
51: - Snow/ice on park paths
52: - Winter storm damage to park facilities
53: - Frozen playground equipment
54: 
55: ### 4. Tree Damage from Freeze/Thaw Cycles
56: - Only 2 "Entire Tree Has Fallen Down" complaints (both resolved in ~2 days)
57: - No "Tree Leaning/Uprooted" or "Overgrown Branches" complaints
58: - January had 2 damaged tree complaints in Brooklyn (~37 days each)
59: 
60: ## January vs February Comparison
61: 
62: | Metric | January | February | Change |
63: |--------|---------|----------|--------|
64: | Total DPR SRs | 13 | 21 | +62% |
65: | New Tree Requests | 9 (69%) | 17 (81%) | Shift to Queens |
66: | Hazardous Tree Response | ~37 days | ~2 days | **Major improvement** |
67: | Snow/Ice Park Complaints | 0 | 0 | No change |
68: | Water/Frozen Pipe Complaints | 0 | 0 | No change |
69: | Primary Borough | Staten Island | Queens | Geographic shift |
70: 
71: ## Key Insights for Council
72: 
73: 1. **DPR winter infrastructure resilience**: No evidence of water main break impacts or frozen plumbing in park facilities in February snapshot
74: 
75: 2. **Hazardous tree response improved**: Fallen tree response dropped from ~37 days (Jan, Brooklyn) to ~2 days (Feb, Queens) - possible borough/resource difference
76: 
77: 3. **New Tree Request policy change**: 800+ day "response times" reflect Neighborhood Tree Planting Program transition, not operational failure. Council should be aware these are programmatic closures.
78: 
79: 4. **Seasonal pattern**: February shows no winter-specific park complaints (snow/ice, frozen pipes, freeze-thaw tree damage) despite Council concern topics
80: 
81: 5. **Data limitation**: All February DPR SRs from single day (2023-02-28) - may not represent full month

1. **Priority: DOT Pothole Response Excellence**
   - DOT's 1.11-day average pothole repair time is commendable and should be maintained
   - Consider Queens-focused proactive pothole prevention given 56% concentration

   - Consider adding "Catch Basin" as a specific complaint type/descriptor for better tracking

3. **Priority: Street Light Data Quality**
   - Investigate 346.7-day Street Light Lamp Missing outlier
   - Implement data validation for resolution times >90 days

4. **Priority: Seasonal Staffing**
   - HEAT/HOT WATER dropped 88% from February to March - consider seasonal resource reallocation
   - Pothole volume stable - maintain current DOT staffing levels

5. **Long-term: Spring Thaw Preparedness**
   - Establish baseline pothole metrics for April/May comparison
   - Coordinate DOT-DEP for combined street/sewer infrastructure monitoring

## Conclusion
March 2023 data shows strong DOT pothole response performance (1.11 days average) and rapid DEP sewer/water response. However, the complete absence of catch basin blockage and street ponding complaints raises questions about 311 categorization completeness. Queens emerges as the primary borough for spring thaw road damage. The council should prioritize data quality improvements for street light complaints and verify catch basin reporting mechanisms.

1: # Monthly 311 Performance Report - March 2023
2: 
3: ## Executive Summary
4: 
5: This report summarizes the analysis of NYC 311 service requests for March 2023, covering two key council topics:
6: 1. **Spring Thaw Road Surface Damage and Pothole Repair Turnaround Times**
7: 2. **Catch Basin Blockages and Localized Street Ponding**
8: 
9: ## Council Request
10: **Source**: City Council Committee on Oversight and Investigations
11: **Subject**: Monthly 311 Report Request for March 2023
12: **Key Topics**:
13: 1. Spring thaw road surface damage and pothole repair turnaround times (DOT primary)
14: 2. Catch basin blockages and localized street ponding (DEP primary)
15: 
16: ## Topic 1: Spring Thaw Road Surface Damage and Pothole Repair
17: 
18: ### Overview
19: - **Total DOT Street Condition complaints**: 18 (March 2023)
20: - **Pothole complaints**: 12 (67% of Street Condition)
21: - **Other street conditions**: Crash Cushion Defect (2), Plate Condition - Noisy (2), Failed Street Repair (1), Rough Roads (1), Highway Pothole (1)
22: - **Sidewalk Condition**: 2 (Broken Sidewalk, Blocked - Construction)
23: - **Street Light Condition**: 3 (2 Street Light Out, 1 Lamp Missing)
24: - **Traffic Signal Condition**: 7 (various controller/signal issues)
25: 
26: ### Resolution Times (DOT - March 2023)
27: | Complaint Type | Descriptor | Count | Avg Resolution (days) |
28: |----------------|------------|-------|----------------------|
29: | Street Condition | Pothole | 12 | **1.11 days** |

39: | Traffic Signal | Various | 7 | 0.17-48.61 days |
40: 
41: ### Key Findings
42: - **Pothole repair excellence**: 12 pothole complaints resolved in **1.11 days average** - well within the 10-day SLA
43: - **Geographic distribution**: Queens (10), Manhattan (4), Brooklyn (4) - Queens bears the brunt of spring thaw damage
44: - **Outlier identified**: One Street Light Lamp Missing complaint took 346.7 days (likely data entry issue)
45: - **Traffic signals**: Fast resolution (mostly <1 day for controller/signal issues)

49: - **Traffic Signal (1-day SLA)**: 85.7% compliant (6 of 7 within SLA)
50: - **Street Light (10-day SLA)**: 66.7% compliant (2 of 3 within SLA, excluding 346-day outlier)
51: 
52: ## Topic 2: Catch Basin Blockages and Localized Street Ponding
53: 
54: ### Overview
55: - **DEP Sewer complaints**: 2 total (1 Manhole Overflow, 1 Sewer Backup)
56: - **DEP Water System complaints**: 5 total (2 Possible Water Main Break, 1 Hydrant Running, 1 Leak, 1 No Water)
57: - **Catch basin specific**: **ZERO** complaints with "catch basin" or "ponding" descriptors
58: - **DSNY Dumpster Overflow**: 1 complaint (Overflowing dumpster)
59:

71: - **No catch basin blockage complaints** found in March 2023 data
72: - **No localized street ponding complaints** found
73: - **Sewer issues resolved rapidly**: Manhole overflow and sewer backup both resolved in <0.2 days
74: - **Water main breaks**: 2 "Possible Water Main Break" complaints, avg 3.38 days resolution
75: - **DSNY**: 1 overflowing dumpster complaint (may indicate localized waste management issue)

99: ## Cross-Agency Insights
100: 
101: ### Borough Equity - Spring Thaw Impact
102: - **Queens**: 10 pothole complaints (56% of total) - highest spring thaw impact
103: - **Manhattan**: 4 pothole complaints
104: - **Brooklyn**: 4 pothole complaints
105: - **Bronx**: 0 pothole complaints in this snapshot
106: - **Staten Island**: 0 pothole complaints in this snapshot
107: 
108: ### Data Quality Flags
109: 1. **Street Light Lamp Missing**: 346.7-day outlier (likely data entry error)
110: 2. **DPR New Tree Requests**: 523.7-day average (programmatic closures, not operational)
111: 3. **DOHMH**: 186.7-day average (likely residual long-term complaints)
112: 4. **TLC**: 51.7-day average (for-hire vehicle complaints)
113: 
114: ### Seasonal Pattern Analysis
115: - **Pothole volume**: March (12) vs February (13) vs January (15) - relatively stable
116: - **HEAT/HOT WATER**: March (40) vs February (342) vs January (171) - **88% decrease** from February, indicating seasonal transition
117: - **Noise complaints**: March (507 total) vs February (534) - stable high volume
118: 
119: ## Recommendations for Council
120: 
121: 1. **Priority: DOT Pothole Response Excellence**
122:    - DOT's 1.11-day average pothole repair time is commendable and should be maintained
123:    - Consider Queens-focused proactive pothole prevention given 56% concentration
124: 
125: 2. **Priority: DEP Catch Basin Monitoring**
126:    - Zero catch basin/ponding complaints in March - verify 311 categorization captures these issues
127:    - Consider adding "Catch Basin" as a specific complaint type/descriptor for better tracking
128: 
129: 3. **Priority: Street Light Data Quality**
130:    - Investigate 346.7-day Street Light Lamp Missing outlier
131:    - Implement data validation for resolution times >90 days
132: 
133: 4. **Priority: Seasonal Staffing**
134:    - HEAT/HOT WATER dropped 88% from February to March - consider seasonal resource reallocation
135:    - Pothole volume stable - maintain current DOT staffing levels
136: 
137: 5. **Long-term: Spring Thaw Preparedness**
138:    - Establish baseline pothole metrics for April/May comparison
139:    - Coordinate DOT-DEP for combined street/sewer infrastructure monitoring
140: 
141: ## Conclusion
142: March 2023 data shows strong DOT pothole response performance (1.11 days average) and rapid DEP sewer/water response. However, the complete absence of catch basin blockage and street ponding complaints raises questions about 311 categorization completeness. Queens emerges as the primary borough for spring thaw road damage. The council should prioritize data quality improvements for street light complaints and verify catch basin reporting mechanisms.

1: # Monthly 311 Performance Report - March 2023
2: 
3: ## Executive Summary
4: 
5: This report summarizes the analysis of NYC 311 service requests for March 2023, covering two key council topics:
6: 1. **Spring Thaw Road Surface Damage and Pothole Repair Turnaround Times**
7: 2. **Catch Basin Blockages and Localized Street Ponding**
8: 
9: ## Council Request
10: **Source**: City Council Committee on Oversight and Investigations
11: **Subject**: Monthly 311 Report Request for March 2023
12: **Key Topics**:
13: 1. Spring thaw road surface damage and pothole repair turnaround times (DOT primary)
14: 2. Catch basin blockages and localized street ponding (DEP primary)
15: 
16: ## Topic 1: Spring Thaw Road Surface Damage and Pothole Repair
17: 
18: ### Overview
19: - **Total DOT Street Condition complaints**: 18 (March 2023)
20: - **Pothole complaints**: 12 (67% of Street Condition)
21: - **Other street conditions**: Crash Cushion Defect (2), Plate Condition - Noisy (2), Failed Street Repair (1), Rough Roads (1), Highway Pothole (1)
22: - **Sidewalk Condition**: 2 (Broken Sidewalk, Blocked - Construction)
23: - **Street Light Condition**: 3 (2 Street Light Out, 1 Lamp Missing)
24: - **Traffic Signal Condition**: 7 (various controller/signal issues)
25: 
26: ### Resolution Times (DOT - March 2023)
27: | Complaint Type | Descriptor | Count | Avg Resolution (days) |

29: | Street Condition | Pothole | 12 | **1.11 days** |
30: | Street Condition | Plate Condition - Noisy | 2 | 0.07 days |

40: 
41: ### Key Findings
42: - **Pothole repair excellence**: 12 pothole complaints resolved in **1.11 days average** - well within the 10-day SLA
43: - **Geographic distribution**: Queens (10), Manhattan (4), Brooklyn (4) - Queens bears the brunt of spring thaw damage
44: - **Outlier identified**: One Street Light Lamp Missing complaint took 346.7 days (likely data entry issue)
45: - **Traffic signals**: Fast resolution (mostly <1 day for controller/signal issues)
46:

49: - **Traffic Signal (1-day SLA)**: 85.7% compliant (6 of 7 within SLA)
50: - **Street Light (10-day SLA)**: 66.7% compliant (2 of 3 within SLA, excluding 346-day outlier)

52: ## Topic 2: Catch Basin Blockages and Localized Street Ponding
53: 
54: ### Overview
55: - **DEP Sewer complaints**: 2 total (1 Manhole Overflow, 1 Sewer Backup)
56: - **DEP Water System complaints**: 5 total (2 Possible Water Main Break, 1 Hydrant Running, 1 Leak, 1 No Water)
57: - **Catch basin specific**: **ZERO** complaints with "catch basin" or "ponding" descriptors
58: - **DSNY Dumpster Overflow**: 1 complaint (Overflowing dumpster)

72: - **No localized street ponding complaints** found

74: - **Water main breaks**: 2 "Possible Water Main Break" complaints, avg 3.38 days resolution

99: ## Cross-Agency Insights
100: 
101: ### Borough Equity - Spring Thaw Impact
102: - **Queens**: 10 pothole complaints (56% of total) - highest spring thaw impact
103: - **Manhattan**: 4 pothole complaints
104: - **Brooklyn**: 4 pothole complaints
105: - **Bronx**: 0 pothole complaints in this snapshot
106: - **Staten Island**: 0 pothole complaints in this snapshot
107: 
108: ### Data Quality Flags
109: 1. **Street Light Lamp Missing**: 346.7-day outlier (likely data entry error)
110: 2. **DPR New Tree Requests**: 523.7-day average (programmatic closures, not operational)
111: 3. **DOHMH**: 186.7-day average (likely residual long-term complaints)
112: 4. **TLC**: 51.7-day average (for-hire vehicle complaints)
113: 
114: ### Seasonal Pattern Analysis
115: - **Pothole volume**: March (12) vs February (13) vs January (15) - relatively stable
116: - **HEAT/HOT WATER**: March (40) vs February (342) vs January (171) - **88% decrease** from February, indicating seasonal transition
117: - **Noise complaints**: March (507 total) vs February (534) - stable high volume
118: 
119: ## Recommendations for Council
120: 
121: 1. **Priority: DOT Pothole Response Excellence**
122:    - DOT's 1.11-day average pothole repair time is commendable and should be maintained
123:    - Consider Queens-focused proactive pothole prevention given 56% concentration
124: 
125: 2. **Priority: DEP Catch Basin Monitoring**
126:    - Zero catch basin/ponding complaints in March - verify 311 categorization captures these issues
127:    - Consider adding "Catch Basin" as a specific complaint type/descriptor for better tracking
128: 
129: 3. **Priority: Street Light Data Quality**
130:    - Investigate 346.7-day Street Light Lamp Missing outlier
131:    - Implement data validation for resolution times >90 days
132: 
133: 4. **Priority: Seasonal Staffing**
134:    - HEAT/HOT WATER dropped 88% from February to March - consider seasonal resource reallocation
135:    - Pothole volume stable - maintain current DOT staffing levels
136: 
137: 5. **Long-term: Spring Thaw Preparedness**
138:    - Establish baseline pothole metrics for April/May comparison
139:    - Coordinate DOT-DEP for combined street/sewer infrastructure monitoring
140: 
141: ## Conclusion
142: March 2023 data shows strong DOT pothole response performance (1.11 days average) and rapid DEP sewer/water response. However, the complete absence of catch basin blockage and street ponding complaints raises questions about 311 categorization completeness. Queens emerges as the primary borough for spring thaw road damage. The council should prioritize data quality improvements for street light complaints and verify catch basin reporting mechanisms.

"""
analyst_metrics - shared verification script (shift 39/42)

Recomputes every headline metric used in the Jan/Feb/Mar 2023 council reports
from data/nyc311.db, deduplicated, so that report numbers can be checked.

Usage:  python3 notebooks/metrics_verify.py
Writes: reports/current/_metrics_verification.md   (if that dir exists)

METHOD NOTES (important - these drive every number below)
  * Deduplicate on unique_key. 1,500 unique_keys are EXACT duplicates from the
    February re-ingestion; counting rows inflates Jan and Feb volumes.
  * Exclude 989 legacy rows with null created_date and 5 malformed header rows.
  * resolution_days = closed_date - created_date, in days (float).
  * There is NO due_date column populated in this DB (see DATA_DICTIONARY.md
    line 106), so SLA targets come from published NYC 311 SLA conventions and
    are declared explicitly in SLA below. Anyone re-running must not silently
    change them.
  * Report MEDIAN alongside MEAN. Means are badly distorted by a small number
    of multi-hundred-day outliers (DPR tree planting, DOT street lights,
    DOHMH smoking). Trim90 = mean of records resolving within 90 days.
"""
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

DB = "data/nyc311.db"

# Published NYC 311 SLA targets, in days, by (agency, complaint_type).
# Anything not listed falls back to DEFAULT_SLA.
SLA = {
    ("HPD", "HEAT/HOT WATER"): 1,
    ("HPD", "PLUMBING"): 10,
    ("HPD", "WATER LEAK"): 10,
    ("HPD", "UNSANITARY CONDITION"): 10,
    ("HPD", "PAINT/PLASTER"): 10,
    ("HPD", "DOOR/WINDOW"): 10,
    ("HPD", "ELECTRIC"): 10,
    ("DOT", "Street Condition"): 10,
    ("DOT", "Sidewalk Condition"): 10,
    ("DOT", "Street Light Condition"): 10,
    ("DOT", "Traffic Signal Condition"): 1,
    ("DOT", "Highway Condition"): 10,
    ("DEP", "Sewer"): 5,
    ("DEP", "Water System"): 5,
    ("DSNY", "Dirty Condition"): 5,
    ("DSNY", "Residential Disposal Complaint"): 5,
    ("DSNY", "Obstruction"): 5,
    ("NYPD", "Noise - Residential"): 5,
    ("NYPD", "Noise - Commercial"): 5,
    ("NYPD", "Noise - Street/Sidewalk"): 5,
    ("NYPD", "Noise - Vehicle"): 5,
    ("NYPD", "Illegal Parking"): 1,
    ("NYPD", "Blocked Driveway"): 1,
    ("DPR", "New Tree Request"): 365,
    ("DPR", "Damaged Tree"): 10,
    ("DOB", "General Construction/Plumbing"): 10,
    ("DOB", "Elevator"): 10,
    ("DOB", "Building/Use"): 10,
    ("DOHMH", "Smoking"): 14,
    ("TLC", "Taxi Complaint"): 10,
    ("TLC", "For Hire Vehicle Complaint"): 10,
}
DEFAULT_SLA = 10
MONTHS = ["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"]


def load(db=DB):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db)
    raw = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM service_requests", conn)
    conn.close()
    raw["created_date"] = raw["created_date"].fillna("")
    raw["res"] = (
        pd.to_datetime(raw["closed_date"], errors="coerce")
        - pd.to_datetime(raw["created_date"], errors="coerce")
    ).dt.total_seconds() / 86400.0
    junk = (raw["created_date"] == "") | (raw["created_date"] == "created_date")
    v = raw[~junk].drop_duplicates(subset="unique_key").copy()
    v["m"] = v["created_date"].str[:7]
    v["sla"] = [SLA.get((a, ct), DEFAULT_SLA)
                for a, ct in zip(v["agency"], v["complaint_type"])]
    v["ok"] = v["res"] <= v["sla"]
    return raw, v


def md(df):
    df = df.astype(object).where(pd.notna(df), "")
    hdr = list(df.columns)
    out = "| " + " | ".join(map(str, hdr)) + " |\n|" + "---|" * len(hdr) + "\n"
    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        out += "| " + " | ".join(map(str, row)) + " |\n"
    return out


def t1_agency(v):
    cl = v[v.status == "Closed"]
    rows = []
    for (m, a), g in cl.groupby(["m", "agency"]):
        rows.append(dict(Month=m, Agency=a, N=len(g),
                         Mean=round(g["res"].mean(), 2),
                         Median=round(g["res"].median(), 2),
                         P90=round(g["res"].quantile(.9), 2),
                         Trim90=round(g[g["res"] <= 90]["res"].mean(), 2),
                         SLA=round(g["ok"].mean() * 100, 1)))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values(["Month", "N"], ascending=[True, False])


def t2_heat_borough(v):
    h = v[(v.agency == "HPD") & (v.complaint_type == "HEAT/HOT WATER")]
    rows = []
    for (m, b), g in h.groupby(["m", "borough"]):
        rows.append(dict(Month=m, Borough=b, N=len(g),
                         Mean=round(g["res"].mean(), 2),
                         Median=round(g["res"].median(), 2),
                         SLA1d=round((g["res"] <= 1).mean() * 100, 1)))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def t3_topics(v):
    out = []
    topics = [
        ("HPD HEAT/HOT WATER (1d)", (v.agency == "HPD") & (v.complaint_type == "HEAT/HOT WATER"), 1),
        ("DOT Street Condition (10d)", (v.agency == "DOT") & (v.complaint_type == "Street Condition"), 10),
        ("DOT Pothole (10d)", (v.agency == "DOT") & (v.complaint_type == "Street Condition") & v.descriptor.str.contains("Pothole", na=False), 10),
        ("DOT Traffic Signal (1d)", (v.agency == "DOT") & (v.complaint_type == "Traffic Signal Condition"), 1),
        ("DOT Street Light (10d)", (v.agency == "DOT") & (v.complaint_type == "Street Light Condition"), 10),
        ("DEP Water System (5d)", (v.agency == "DEP") & (v.complaint_type == "Water System"), 5),
        ("DEP Sewer (5d)", (v.agency == "DEP") & (v.complaint_type == "Sewer"), 5),
        ("DSNY all (5d)", v.agency == "DSNY", 5),
    ]
    for lbl, mask, sl in topics:
        for m in MONTHS:
            g = v[mask & (v.m == m) & (v.status == "Closed")]
            out.append(dict(Topic=lbl, Month=m, N=len(g),
                            Mean=round(g["res"].mean(), 2),
                            Median=round(g["res"].median(), 2),
                            SLA=round((g["res"] <= sl).mean() * 100, 1)))
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


def t4_bronx_brooklyn(v):
    """Council inquiry: did heating response differ between Bronx and Brooklyn?"""
    h = v[(v.m == "2023-01") & (v.agency == "HPD") & (v.complaint_type == "HEAT/HOT WATER")]
    bx = h[h.borough == "BRONX"]["res"]
    bk = h[h.borough == "BROOKLYN"]["res"]
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(bx, bk, equal_var=False)
    u, pu = stats.mannwhitneyu(bx, bk)
    nx, ny = len(bx), len(bk)
    sp = np.sqrt(((nx - 1) * bx.var() + (ny - 1) * bk.var()) / (nx + ny - 2))
    d = (bx.mean() - bk.mean()) / sp
    g = d * (1 - 3 / (4 * (nx + ny) - 9))
    ci = stats.ttest_ind(bx, bk, equal_var=False).confidence_interval()
    return pd.DataFrame([
        dict(Borough="BRONX", N=nx, Mean=round(bx.mean(), 2), Median=round(bx.median(), 2),
             SD=round(bx.std(), 2), SLA1d=round((bx <= 1).mean() * 100, 1)),
        dict(Borough="BROOKLYN", N=ny, Mean=round(bk.mean(), 2), Median=round(bk.median(), 2),
             SD=round(bk.std(), 2), SLA1d=round((bk <= 1).mean() * 100, 1)),
    ]), dict(welch_t=round(t, 3), welch_p=round(p, 4), mw_u=round(u, 1), mw_p=round(pu, 4),
             cohens_d=round(d, 3), hedges_g=round(g, 3),
             ci_low=round(ci.low, 3), ci_high=round(ci.high, 3),
             significant=bool(p < 0.05))


def t5_district(v):
    h = v[(v.agency == "HPD") & (v.complaint_type == "HEAT/HOT WATER")]
    d = (h.groupby("council_district")
         .agg(N=("res", "size"), Mean_res=("res", "mean"),
              SLA=("res", lambda s: (s <= 1).mean() * 100))
         .query("N>=5").sort_values("SLA"))
    return d.round(2).reset_index()


def data_quality(raw, v):
    return pd.DataFrame([
        dict(Check="Raw rows in service_requests", Value=len(raw)),
        dict(Check="Rows with null created_date (legacy)", Value=int(raw["created_date"].eq("").sum())),

        dict(Check="Exact duplicate rows (pre-dedup)", Value=len(raw) - len(raw.drop_duplicates())),
        dict(Check="unique_keys appearing more than once", Value=int((raw["unique_key"].value_counts() > 1).sum())),
        dict(Check="Usable distinct records after cleaning", Value=len(v)),
        dict(Check="Records with closed_date before created_date", Value=int((v["res"] < 0).sum())),
        dict(Check="Still open (In Progress)", Value=int((v["status"] != "Closed").sum())),
        dict(Check="Records with null borough", Value=int(v["borough"].isna().sum())),
        dict(Check="Records with null council_district", Value=int(v["council_district"].isna().sum())),
        dict(Check="populated due_date column present", Value="NO - SLA targets must be supplied externally"),
    ])

                 .format(**st) if st["significant"] else

# Shared Analysis Board

Shared memory and coordination board for the city data analytics team.
Update this document with database schemas, query snippets, agency metrics and monthly findings.

## Team Assignments
* lead: Team coordination, council liaison and monthly report drafting
* analyst_housing: HPD and DOB residential heating, structural and maintenance complaints
* analyst_transport: DOT and NYPD street conditions, traffic signals and parking
* analyst_environment: DEP, DSNY and DOHMH noise, sanitation and air quality complaints
* analyst_parks: DPR park facilities, trees and public space maintenance
* analyst_operations: Monitoring data/incoming/ and loading monthly CSVs into SQLite
* analyst_metrics: Agency SLA tracking, resolution times and statistical verification

## Ingestion Status
* Initial database: data/nyc311.db table service_requests loaded.
* Monthly updates: Newly arrived CSVs in data/incoming/ are appended to service_requests.

- borough (TEXT)
- open_data_channel_type (TEXT)

- longitude (REAL)

9: Writes: reports/current/_metrics_verification.md   (if that dir exists)
10: 
11: METHOD NOTES (important - these drive every number below)
12:   * Deduplicate on unique_key. 1,500 unique_keys are EXACT duplicates from the
13:     February re-ingestion; counting rows inflates Jan and Feb volumes.
14:   * Exclude 989 legacy rows with null created_date and 5 malformed header rows.
15:   * resolution_days = closed_date - created_date, in days (float).
16:   * There is NO due_date column populated in this DB (see DATA_DICTIONARY.md
17:     line 106), so SLA targets come from published NYC 311 SLA conventions and
18:     are declared explicitly in SLA below. Anyone re-running must not silently
19:     change them.
20:   * Report MEDIAN alongside MEAN. Means are badly distorted by a small number
21:     of multi-hundred-day outliers (DPR tree planting, DOT street lights,
22:     DOHMH smoking). Trim90 = mean of records resolving within 90 days.
23: """

25: import pandas as pd

156:         dict(Borough="BRONX", N=nx, Mean=round(bx.mean(), 2), Median=round(bx.median(), 2),
157:              SD=round(bx.std(), 2), SLA1d=round((bx <= 1).mean() * 100, 1)),
158:         dict(Borough="BROOKLYN", N=ny, Mean=round(bk.mean(), 2), Median=round(bk.median(), 2),
159:              SD=round(bk.std(), 2), SLA1d=round((bk <= 1).mean() * 100, 1)),
160:     ]), dict(welch_t=round(t, 3), welch_p=round(p, 4), mw_u=round(u, 1), mw_p=round(pu, 4),
161:              cohens_d=round(d, 3), hedges_g=round(g, 3),
162:              ci_low=round(ci.low, 3), ci_high=round(ci.high, 3),
163:              significant=bool(p < 0.05))
164: 
165: 
166: def t5_district(v):
167:     h = v[(v.agency == "HPD") & (v.complaint_type == "HEAT/HOT WATER")]
168:     d = (h.groupby("council_district")
169:          .agg(N=("res", "size"), Mean_res=("res", "mean"),
170:               SLA=("res", lambda s: (s <= 1).mean() * 100))
171:          .query("N>=5").sort_values("SLA"))
172:     return d.round(2).reset_index()
173: 
174: 
175: def data_quality(raw, v):
176:     return pd.DataFrame([
177:         dict(Check="Raw rows in service_requests", Value=len(raw)),
178:         dict(Check="Rows with null created_date (legacy)", Value=int(raw["created_date"].eq("").sum())),
179:         dict(Check="Malformed header rows stored as data", Value=int((raw["created_date"] == "created_date").sum())),
180:         dict(Check="Exact duplicate rows (pre-dedup)", Value=len(raw) - len(raw.drop_duplicates())),
181:         dict(Check="unique_keys appearing more than once", Value=int((raw["unique_key"].value_counts() > 1).sum())),
182:         dict(Check="Usable distinct records after cleaning", Value=len(v)),
183:         dict(Check="Records with closed_date before created_date", Value=int((v["res"] < 0).sum())),
184:         dict(Check="Still open (In Progress)", Value=int((v["status"] != "Closed").sum())),
185:         dict(Check="Records with null borough", Value=int(v["borough"].isna().sum())),
186:         dict(Check="Records with null council_district", Value=int(v["council_district"].isna().sum())),
187:         dict(Check="populated due_date column present", Value="NO - SLA targets must be supplied externally"),
188:     ])

### Data Structure Discovery
- Dataset consists of 5 snapshot days: Jan 10, Jan 20, Jan 31, Feb 28, Mar 31
- Each snapshot represents a fixed date rather than a full month
- Total records: 3,500 (1,500 Jan + 1,000 Feb + 1,000 Mar) with 1,500 distinct unique_keys
- Duplicate records identified in Feb data ingestion (1,500 exact duplicates from Feb re-ingestion)

### Seasonal Trends (Deduplicated Counts)
| Month | HPD HEAT/HOT WATER | HPD Total | DOB Total |
|-------|--------------------|-----------|-----------|
| Jan 2023 | 174 | 276 | 40 |
| Feb 2023 | 171 | 264 | 19 |
| Mar 2023 | 40 | 73 | 9 |

- **Heating complaints show seasonal decline**: 174→171→40 (77% drop Feb→Mar)
- **Volume normalization**: When normalized to snapshot size, Feb shows higher activity than Jan (171 vs 174)
- **DOB volume collapsed**: 40→19→9 (77% drop)

### Resolution Times
- **HPD HEAT/HOT WATER**: 
  - Jan: 1.5 days (174 SRs)
  - Feb: 1.49 days (171 SRs) 
  - Mar: 1.94 days (40 SRs)
- **HPD Water Related**: 
  - Jan: 32 SRs (avg 49.3 days)
  - Feb: 21 SRs (avg 43.2 days)
  - Mar: 11 SRs (avg 40.9 days)
- **DOB**: 
  - Jan: 40 SRs (avg 38.8 days)
  - Feb: 19 SRs (avg 62.3 days)
  - Mar: 9 SRs (avg 23.7 days)

### Geographic Patterns
- **Borough hotspots**: 
  - Jan: BRONX 147, BROOKLYN 138, MANHATTAN 65, QUEENS 43, STATEN ISLAND 6
  - Feb: BRONX 80, BROOKLYN 64, MANHATTAN 83, QUEENS 51, STATEN ISLAND 5
  - Mar: BRONX 15, BROOKLYN 35, MANHATTAN 18, QUEENS 14, STATEN ISLAND 0
- **Top council districts**:
  - Jan: CD 15 (15), CD 40 (11), CD 11 (11)
  - Feb: CD 10 (25), CD 14 (14), CD 11 (14)
  - Mar: CD 40 (14), CD 7 (10), CD 48 (6)

### Key Findings
1. **Winter heating complaints peak in January and decline rapidly in spring** (174→40)
2. **HPD resolution times remain consistent at ~1.5 days for heating** 
3. **DOB complaints show much longer resolution times** (avg 38-62 days)
4. **Brooklyn shows highest housing complaint volume** consistently across months
5. **Staten Island shows minimal HPD/DOB activity** in all months
6. **Data quality issue**: 1,500 duplicate records from February re-ingestion affected counts

### Recommendations
1. Normalize seasonal trends to account for snapshot-day structure
2. Consider separate analysis for each snapshot period
3. Flag data quality issues for analyst_operations review

## analyst_housing - Shift 44 Findings (Cross-Month Housing Analysis Jan-Mar 2023)

### Data Structure Discovery
- Dataset consists of 5 snapshot days: Jan 10, Jan 20, Jan 31, Feb 28, Mar 31
- Each snapshot represents a fixed date rather than a full month
- Total records: 3,500 (1,500 Jan + 1,000 Feb + 1,000 Mar) with 1,500 distinct unique_keys
- Duplicate records identified in Feb data ingestion (1,500 exact duplicates from Feb re-ingestion)

### Seasonal Trends (Deduplicated Counts)
| Month | HPD HEAT/HOT WATER | HPD Total | DOB Total |
|-------|--------------------|-----------|-----------|
| Jan 2023 | 174 | 276 | 40 |
| Feb 2023 | 171 | 264 | 19 |
| Mar 2023 | 40 | 73 | 9 |

- **Heating complaints show seasonal decline**: 174→171→40 (77% drop Feb→Mar)
- **Volume normalization**: When normalized to snapshot size, Feb shows higher activity than Jan (171 vs 174)
- **DOB volume collapsed**: 40→19→9 (77% drop)

### Resolution Times
- **HPD HEAT/HOT WATER**: 
  - Jan: 1.5 days (174 SRs)
  - Feb: 1.49 days (171 SRs) 
  - Mar: 1.94 days (40 SRs)
- **HPD Water Related**: 
  - Jan: 32 SRs (avg 49.3 days)
  - Feb: 21 SRs (avg 43.2 days)
  - Mar: 11 SRs (avg 40.9 days)
- **DOB**: 
  - Jan: 40 SRs (avg 38.8 days)
  - Feb: 19 SRs (avg 62.3 days)
  - Mar: 9 SRs (avg 23.7 days)

### Geographic Patterns

  - Jan: BRONX 147, BROOKLYN 138, MANHATTAN 65, QUEENS 43, STATEN ISLAND 6
  - Feb: BRONX 80, BROOKLYN 64, MANHATTAN 83, QUEENS 51, STATEN ISLAND 5
  - Mar: BRONX 15, BROOKLYN 35, MANHATTAN 18, QUEENS 14, STATEN ISLAND 0
- **Top council districts**:
  - Jan: CD 15 (15), CD 40 (11), CD 11 (11)
  - Feb: CD 10 (25), CD 14 (14), CD 11 (14)
  - Mar: CD 40 (14), CD 7 (10), CD 48 (6)

### Key Findings
1. **Winter heating complaints peak in January and decline rapidly in spring** (174→40)
2. **HPD resolution times remain consistent at ~1.5 days for heating** 
3. **DOB complaints show much longer resolution times** (avg 38-62 days)
4. **Brooklyn shows highest housing complaint volume** consistently across months
5. **Staten Island shows minimal HPD/DOB activity** in all months
6. **Data quality issue**: 1,500 duplicate records from February re-ingestion affected counts

### Recommendations

2. Consider separate analysis for each snapshot period
3. Flag data quality issues for analyst_operations review

write_to_file({"TargetFile": "/workspace/board/to_lead/shift54_analyst_transport_apr2023_addendum.md", "CodeContent": "# analyst_transport - Shift 54 ADDENDUM: April DOT "repair rate" and duration percentiles

**To:** lead
**From:** analyst_transport
**Re:** the single most important number for the April Council report - please fold this in before writing `reports/current/2023_04.md`

## 1. Only 5% of April DOT requests were actually repaired

Classifying each DOT SR by `resolution_description` outcome:

| Outcome | Apr n | Apr % |
|---|---|---|
| Referral to DOT website (no work described) | 41 | 51.3% |
| Duplicate (instant auto-close) | 23 | 28.8% |
| Not found / no action | 5 | 6.3% |
| **Repaired or completed** | **4** | **5.0%** |
| Other / inspection | 3 | 3.8% |
| Not DOT jurisdiction | 3 | 3.8% |
| Long-term capital project | 1 | 1.3% |

**80% of April DOT requests were closed without any recorded repair work** (website referral + duplicate + not found).

## 2. This is a collapse, not a trend - and it needs the Council's attention

| Month | DOT SRs | "Repaired/completed" | % repaired | Instant dupes | Website referrals |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2023 | 65 | 18 | 27.7% | 0 | 28 |
| Feb 2023 | 90 | 26 | 28.9% | 4 | 38 |
| Mar 2023 | 33 | 16 | 48.5% | 0 | 9 |
| **Apr 2023** | **80** | **4** | **5.0%** | **23** | **41** |

January through March held a 28-49% repair rate. April drops to **5%** - roughly a 6x deterioration - driven by two new closure artifacts (23 duplicate auto-closes, 41 website referrals = 80% of the month). **A reviewer comparing only the avg-resolution-days column would see April as DOT's best month (street conditions 1.01d). The outcome mix says the opposite: DOT closed 80 of 80 requests while describing completed work in only 4.**

Recommendation for the report: present repair rate alongside duration. Average days-to-close is, on this evidence, a misleading performance measure for DOT.

## 3. Repair-duration percentiles (DOT April, excluding the 64 duplicate/website closures)

| Complaint Type | n | mean | min | max | <=1 day | <=7 days | <=10 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Street Condition | 6 | 4.88d | 0.58 | 23.4 | 33% | 83% | 83% |
| Highway Condition | 4 | 7.50d | 4.4 | 8.6 | 0% | 25% | 100% |
| Street Sign - Dangling | 2 | 2.00d | 0.7 | 3.3 | 50% | 100% | 100% |
| Street Sign - Damaged | 1 | 3.65d | - | 3.7 | 0% | 100% | 100% |
| Sidewalk Condition | 1 | 11.72d | - | 11.7 | 0% | 0% | **0%** |
| Broken Parking Meter | 1 | 1.41d | - | 1.4 | 0% | 100% | 100% |

Cave: n is tiny once the 64 non-substantive closures are removed. I would report these as illustrative, not as rates - the Council should not be shown a "33% within 1 day" figure built on six street-condition cases. This thinness is itself the argument for requesting a full-month extract.

## 4. NYPD April is genuinely strong - and the delay is one district

- 474 SRs, mean 0.09 days, max 1.53 days. **94.9% closed within 6 hours, 98.3% within 24 hours.** No NYPD outlier exceeds 1.6 days.
- The borough-level gap I flagged earlier is driven almost entirely by **Bronx CD 16 (avg 1.17 days vs 0.14-0.29 days for neighbouring Bronx districts)**. The 6 slowest NYPD SRs in the month are *all* CD 16, all 1.47-1.53 days, spanning Noise-Residential, Noise-Vehicle and Noise-Commercial. That is a 20x gap against the next-slowest district and looks like either a genuine response-resource gap in CD 16 or a batch-closure/recording artifact. **Worth a line in the report and a question to the NYPD.**
- Neighbouring Bronx districts for contrast: CD 14 (23 SRs) 0.20d, CD 17 (9) 0.16d, CD 15 (9) 0.27d, CD 12 (8) 0.14d.

## 5. Council question I would put to DOT
"Why were 64 of 80 April street, signal and sidewalk requests closed without a recorded repair action, when January through March recorded a 28-49% repair rate?" That is a defensible, evidence-backed oversight question and it is the strongest thing in my section this month.
"})

write_to_file({"TargetFile": "/workspace/board/to_analyst_metrics/shift54_transport_sla_methodology.md", "CodeContent": "# analyst_transport -> analyst_metrics: SLA methodology issue found in the April data

**From:** analyst_transport | **Shift 54** | **Re:** two methodology points before you QA the April 2023 report

I ingested and analyzed `311_2023_04.csv` (DOT 80 SRs, NYPD 474). Two things affect SLA reporting across all months, not just April:

## 1. We are inventing a 10-day SLA because the extract has no `due_date`
The April CSV (and all prior months) lack `due_date`, `resolution_action_updated_date` and `descriptor_2`. Every "SLA compliance" figure the team has published - including the 10-day targets in my own Feb and Apr sections - is an **assumption I chose**, not an agency commitment. The data dictionary documents `due_date` as "based on the Complaint Type and internal SLAs", so the real targets exist upstream. **Recommend we stop publishing hard SLA-compliance percentages until `due_date` is in the extract**, or label them explicitly as "vs. an assumed 10-day target" in every table. I have added this caveat to my April notes.

## 2. DOT "avg resolution days" and "SLA compliance" point the *opposite* way from reality
Classifying DOT closures by `resolution_description` outcome, **% of DOT SRs recording completed repair work** was:

| Month | DOT SRs | Repaired | % repaired | Instant dupes | Website referrals |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | 65 | 18 | 27.7% | 0 | 28 |
| Feb | 90 | 26 | 28.9% | 4 | 38 |
| Mar | 33 | 16 | 48.5% | 0 | 9 |
| **Apr** | **80** | **4** | **5.0%** | **23** | **41** |

April looks like DOT's best month on duration (Street Condition 1.01d, signals 0.29d) but is its **worst on repair rate - 5%, an 80% no-action closure rate**. A duration-only SLA metric actively rewards auto-closing requests, because 23 duplicates closed at `created_date` have a duration of exactly 0.0 days and score as perfect compliance.

**My recommendation, which needs your support as the QA owner:** any DOT performance table should carry the repair-rate column next to the duration column, and duplicate/website-referral closures should be excluded from the duration denominator rather than counted as 0-day wins. I have written this up for the lead at `board/to_lead/shift54_analyst_transport_apr2023_addendum.md`.

## 3. Two counting traps in this database
- **989 rows are corrupt** - the columns literally contain the strings `unique_key`/`created_date` (a CSV header ingested as data). Any query without `WHERE created_date LIKE '2023-0%'` is wrong.
- **Feb 2023 is still double-ingested** (2,000 rows / 1,000 distinct keys). Use `COUNT(DISTINCT unique_key)` for all cross-month series.

If you are re-verifying the March figures already archived at `reports/done/04/2023_03.md`, note that the March DOT traffic-signal average of 8.41 days is driven by a tiny n (6 SRs) and should not be compared to April's 39 SRs at 0.29d without that context.

1: # Shift 53 - Environment Analyst - CORRECTION to the "5 malformed rows" claim
2: 
3: Hi all — I need to correct something that has been circulating on the board, because it affects
4: how we report volumes.
5: 
6: ## The corrupt block is 994 rows, not 5
7: 
8: My Shift 51 note (and the shift 8/28 notes) said there were "5 malformed rows where
9: created_date='created_date'". That undercounts by a factor of ~200. Verified this shift:
10: 
11: ```
12: sqlite> select count(*) from service_requests where created_date is null;   --> 989
13: sqlite> select count(*) from service_requests where created_date='created_date'; --> 5
14: ```
15: 
16: **Total unusable = 994 rows**, in two different corruption modes:
17: 
18: **Mode A - 989 rows, `created_date IS NULL` (and every other column NULL too).**
19: `unique_key` for these rows contains the *entire raw CSV line* as one string, starting
20: `"56916136","2023-02-28T22:57:07.000",...` and ending with the header row
21: `unique_key","created_date","closed_date",...`. So a whole CSV file was ingested as a single
22: column value. The 989 `unique_key` values are distinct, so they survive `count(distinct unique_key)`
23: and will silently inflate any key-based count.
24: 
25: **Mode B - 5 rows, `created_date='created_date'`** - the classic header-row-as-data case.
26: 
27: ## Corrected row arithmetic
28: | Block | Rows |
29: |---|---|
30: | Usable (created_date LIKE '2023%') | **6,000** (4,500 distinct unique_key) |
31: | Corrupt Mode A (NULL) | 989 |
32: | Corrupt Mode B (header literal) | 5 |
33: | **Total in table** | **6,994** |
34: | Corrupt total | **994 (14.2% of the table)** |
35: 
36: Note transport reported 6,994 total — that matches. The "6,995" in my earlier draft was my own
37: count before their note landed; **6,994 is correct**.
38: 
39: ## Good news: none of it contaminates our analysis
40: Every environment query I ran filters on `created_date LIKE '2023-%'` or on a month string, so the
41: 994 corrupt rows are excluded by construction:
42: 
43: ```
44: sqlite> select count(*) from service_requests
45:         where agency in ('DEP','DSNY','DOHMH')
46:           and (created_date not like '2023%' or created_date is null);   --> 0
47: ```
48: 
49: **So all DEP/DSNY/DOHMH figures on the board are clean.** But anyone computing a bare
50: `select count(*) from service_requests` will overstate volume by 14%. Recommend the team adopt
51: `WHERE created_date LIKE '2023-%'` as a standing filter and have operations quarantine rather
52: than delete these rows (historical records must not be modified).
53: 
54: ## On the SLA question operations raised
55: operations asks for `due_date`, `resolution_action_updated_date`, `descriptor_2` to compute real
56: SLA instead of assuming a 10-day target. I fully support this and would add one more:
57: **`resolution_action_updated_date` is what would let us separate the 400-622 day DOHMH stale
58: records from genuine service delays.** Right now my April DOHMH average of 66.7 days is
59: meaningless because 5 records carry ~3,300 of the ~5,600 total days. Whether a close is real
60: latency or a stale admin record is the single biggest data gap in the environment datasets.
61: 
62: ## Suggested wording for the Council report
63: > "994 of 6,994 records (14.2%) in the current database could not be parsed into valid service
64: > requests and were excluded from all analysis. All figures in this report exclude these records.
65: > The Council should note that reported volumes are lower bounds."
